title: Poutine (Fries, Cheese Curds and Gravy)
summary: Double-fried potato batons are piled with fresh cheese curds and a rich stock-based gravy, poured over hot so the curds soften just enough while the fries stay crisp underneath.
equipment: large heavy pot or Dutch oven (at least 5 litres) or a deep fryer
2 rimmed baking trays, one lined with kitchen paper, one with a wire rack

ingredients.item: floury potatoes (such as russet or Maris Piper), peeled
neutral frying oil (sunflower, rapeseed or vegetable)
fresh cheese curds, at room temperature, torn into bite-size pieces
ingredients.note: or torn fresh mozzarella if you cannot find curds

steps.title: Build the gravy base
steps.text: Melt the butter in a saucepan over medium heat and cook the shallot and garlic for 2 minutes until softened. Whisk in the flour and cook for a further 2 minutes until it turns light golden; this brief cooking of flour and butter together removes any raw, pasty taste before the liquid goes in.

steps.title: Simmer the gravy
steps.text: Gradually whisk in the beef and chicken stocks, add the thyme sprigs, and simmer for 10-15 minutes until reduced to about 500 ml and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Off the heat, stir in the vinegar and pepper, tasting before adding any salt since stock brands vary widely in saltiness. Keep the gravy hot while you fry the potatoes.

steps.title: Soak the potato batons
steps.text: Cut the potatoes into 8 mm batons and soak in cold water for at least 1 hour, changing the water until it runs clear. Drain and dry the batons thoroughly; rinsing away excess surface starch like this helps stop the fries sticking together and clouding the oil during frying.

steps.title: First fry at 160°C
steps.text: Heat the frying oil to 160°C and fry the potato batons in batches for about 5 minutes, until pale and limp. Drain each batch on a wire rack; this first fry cooks the batons through gently before the higher heat of the second fry gives them their crust.

steps.title: Second fry at 190°C
steps.text: Raise the oil to 190°C and fry the batons again in batches for 3-4 minutes, until deep golden and crisp. Drain well so the fries stay crunchy once topped.

steps.title: Assemble immediately
steps.text: Pile the hot fries into bowls, scatter over the cheese curds, then pour over the very hot gravy at once. The heat from the fries and gravy together softens the curds just enough to turn gooey at the edges while the centres stay firm; serve straight away, and never leave hot oil unattended.

tips: Use fresh cheese curds at room temperature - cold curds straight from the fridge won't soften properly when the hot gravy hits them.
A common mistake is assembling poutine too early and letting it sit - pour the hot gravy over right before serving so the fries don't go soggy.
Taste the gravy before seasoning with extra salt, since stock brands differ a lot in how salty they already are.
Dry the soaked potato batons thoroughly before frying, or the oil will spit and the fries won't crisp properly.

Frying safety: use a heavy, deep pot no more than half full of oil, with a clip-on thermometer, and dry the food before it goes in. Never leave hot oil unattended. If the oil catches fire, turn off the heat and cover the pot with a metal lid or use a fire extinguisher; never use water.
storage: Poutine is best assembled and eaten immediately, as the fries lose their crispness within minutes. The gravy on its own keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days or frozen for up to 2 months, reheated in a saucepan until piping hot (74°C) before serving over freshly fried potatoes and curds. Cool leftovers in a shallow container and refrigerate within 2 hours (within 1 hour on a day above 32°C).
